core.text: The everyday way to tell someone *not* to do something is **noli / nolite + infinitive (the polite 'don't …')**. *Nōlī* is the command form of *nōlō* (I do not want), so *Nōlī timēre!* is literally 'don't want to fear' — 'don't be afraid'. To several people say *nōlīte*. The verb after it is the plain infinitive (the 'to' form), so a deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks) keeps its -ī / -ārī / -ērī infinitive: *Nōlī imitārī!* Latin name: *prohibitiō: nōlī cum īnfīnītīvō*.
English makes a negative command with *don't* plus the verb: *don't go*. Latin does the same job with a helping verb, 'be unwilling to go'.
nōlī (to one person) or nōlīte (to several) + infinitive = 'do not …'.

*Nōlī* is itself **the imperative (the command form)** of *nōlō*; the real action is the infinitive that follows. So *Nōlī abīre!* pairs with the positive *Abī!* (go away!), not with *nōn abī*, which Latin never says.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 20) call this a 'polite prohibition' and note that *nē* + imperative (*nē timē*) exists but is rare, mostly in poetry. Prose also uses *nē* with **the perfect subjunctive (the 'have done' form: nescio quid fecerit; ne timueris = don't be afraid)**: *nē timuerīs!* — the same meaning, a shade more urgent (chapter XXXII).
Other polite refusals use *cavē* (beware) + subjunctive: *cavē cadās* — mind you don't fall.
